summary: Sets up a permanent registry at IANA for HTTP header field names and a provisional repository for headers that are not yet formally standardized, following the process in RFC 3864. It supplies the initial contents of both so that header names can be tracked in one place.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP headers are labels on web messages. This memo creates an official list of those labels, plus a scratch list for new ones, so people do not accidentally pick the same name.

questions: how do you register a new http header
difference between permanent and provisional http headers
subtitle: The official register of HTTP header field names.

tldr.problem: HTTP headers can be defined by anyone following any RFC, making it hard to know what headers exist, who controls them, or how to register a new one without naming conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC creates a permanent IANA registry of HTTP header field names, listing all standardized headers with their status, author, and RFC specification. It also establishes a provisional repository for headers being proposed but not yet standardized.
tldr.outcome: Developers can now check a single official list before inventing a new header, reducing fragmentation and helping the IETF track what headers are in use across the web.

today: RFC 4229 serves as the baseline inventory of HTTP headers as of December 2005. The IANA registry continues to grow with new headers from HTTP/2, HTTP/3, and various extension specifications. The registration process from RFC 3864 is still used to register new headers today.

sections.title: Why a Registry Matters
sections.content:
The HTTP protocol, defined in RFCs 2616 and other documents, allows for extension headers: new header field names that are not part of the core protocol. This is powerful because it lets the web evolve without waiting for formal standardization.

The problem is that with no central registry, anyone can propose a header, and developers have no easy way to know if a name is already taken or what a header is supposed to do. Someone might invent X-Custom-Header at Company A and someone at Company B might independently invent the same name with different meaning. Or a developer might invent a new header that duplicates one already defined in an RFC they never read.

This RFC solves that problem by creating a permanent registry at IANA (the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) listing all standardized HTTP headers. It also establishes a provisional repository for headers being proposed but not yet official, per the registration procedures in RFC 3864.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP headers are labels on web messages. This memo says: here are all the labels that mean something standard, who invented each one, and where to look for the rules.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Headers
sections.content:
The registry has two categories. Permanent headers are officially standardized and will never be removed. Examples include Accept (the client says what file types it can read), Content-Type (the server says what file type it is sending), Authorization (the client proves who it is), and Cache-Control (the server says how long to save a copy). These are defined in HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, WebDAV, content negotiation, authentication, or other IETF RFCs.

Provisional headers are submitted by developers or companies for tracking and possible future standardization. They are not yet official IETF standards. The registry includes headers like Content-Transfer-Encoding, Message-ID, and Title, which may be useful but are not yet formally defined. Provisional headers may be promoted to permanent status, remain provisional, or eventually be withdrawn if unused.
sections.plainLanguage: Some labels are official and stable (like Accept). Others are being tried out (like my new custom header). The registry has both lists so you can see what is official and what is experimental.

sections.title: What the Registry Contains
sections.content:
For each header, the registry records: the header's name (e.g., Accept); the applicable protocol (HTTP in these cases); the status (standard, informational, experimental, or provisional); the author or change controller (usually the IETF, but sometimes a person or company); and a reference to the specification document that defines the header, typically a specific RFC section.

For example, the Accept header is a permanent, standard header defined in RFC 2616. The Accept-Additions header is permanent but informational and defined in RFC 2324 (an April 1st RFC). The Accept-Features header is experimental and defined in RFC 2295.

The RFC does not attempt to document the syntax or semantics of header values; that is left to each header's specification. It also does not track how a header's meaning might change depending on context (e.g., Cache-Control has different meaning in requests and responses). The registry treats all HTTP header names as a single, unified namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry says: this header exists, here is who invented it, what RFC explains it, and whether it is official or still being tried out.

sections.title: The Permanent Headers
sections.content:
The RFC lists 116 permanent headers, all from established RFCs. They fall into several categories: request headers sent by clients (Accept, Authorization, User-Agent, Cookie); response headers sent by servers (Content-Type, Set-Cookie, Server, Cache-Control); general headers that appear in either requests or responses (Date, Connection, Via); and entity headers describing the body of a message (Content-Length, Content-Encoding, Last-Modified, ETag).

Some headers are from HTTP/1.0 or HTTP/1.1 core; others are from extension RFCs for content negotiation, caching, authentication, compression, or WebDAV file sharing. Together they form the standard vocabulary for HTTP communication, and their registration ensures stable reference and prevents accidental naming conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry lists all the standard labels. Some are for saying what you want (Accept), some are for saying what you are sending (Content-Type), and some are for everything (Date).

sections.title: Provisional and the Future
sections.content:
The RFC also lists 17 provisional headers submitted by individuals or companies for tracking and discussion. These include Content-Transfer-Encoding (how to encode the body for transmission), Message-ID (a unique identifier for the message, borrowed from email), and Title (the title of a web page). Provisional headers allow the community to see what extensions are being tried and to discuss whether they should be standardized.

The registration procedure from RFC 3864 allows anyone to submit a new header for provisional registration, specifying its name, intended use, syntax, and semantics. If the header proves useful and interoperable across implementations, it may be promoted to permanent status. If it falls into disuse, it can be archived. This process lets the web evolve organically while keeping a historical record of what was tried.
sections.plainLanguage: If you invent a new header, you can ask IANA to register it provisionally so others know it exists. If it becomes popular, it might become official later.
